title: Iris and the Jam Tart Avalanche
markdown:
The scent of warm bread, mingling with the sharp tang of ink, always offered Iris the raven a comforting dual embrace. Her office, a cozy nook above The Crumbly Crust bakery, was the historical nerve centre of Blackbird High. Dust motes danced in lamplight like tiny golden acrobats. Iris, school archivist, black feathers gleaming, would straighten a stack of ancient newspapers, quill tucked behind her ear. She cherished the hushed quiet, the predictable rhythm of archival work.

This year a tremor rippled through her usually steady wings. The annual Founder’s Day Fête. And she was in charge — not a small part, the entire operation. A cold dread settled. What if she couldn’t handle it? What if it all went wrong? Her deepest flaw, a desperate need for absolute order, whispered. Chaos felt like drowning.

Headmaster Grimshaw, kindly, tie perpetually askew, had boomed, “Iris, my dear, you’ve got this. Total control. No more incidents.” Last year’s Fête had involved a rogue bouncy castle over the oak trees and pigeons nesting in the chemistry lab. Failure this year meant cancellation. The clock ticked. The town’s excitement ticked with it.

With a flap of determined wings she left the quiet office. Precision was the only answer. She drafted instructions so detailed they would make a master clockmaker weep.

“Every stall must have precisely three balloons,” she dictated to Bartholomew, her new badger assistant, who arrived with an earnest unsettling gleam in his wide eyes. “Tethered at exactly one metre height. No more, no less. The refreshment tent: exactly five hundred miniature jam tarts. Arranged in five neat rows of ten.”

Bartholomew nodded, whiskers twitching with unnerving comprehension, promising to follow every word with the seriousness of a badger digging for truffles.

The Fête grounds transformed — far from Iris’s vision. Bartholomew, having followed her instructions to the letter, had placed exactly three balloons at one metre height on every single table in the main square: a dizzying low-hanging cloud of primary colours. The five hundred jam tarts, meant for neat rows, now formed a precarious towering pyramid, threatening to spill with the slightest breeze. And the Grand Opening Ceremony, where Iris had stated the confetti cannon must be fired with gusto, resulted in a deafening blast that sent pigeons scattering and, as a bonus, the bakery’s ancient chimney pot tumbling with a resounding clatter.

Iris’s heart hammered. Her ordered world unravelled. Squawks, delighted shrieks, the ominous crunch of falling jam tarts. Bartholomew, beaming with innocent pride, chirped, “Just like you wrote, Archivist Iris! Everything is perfect!” Heat rose. Feathers bristled. She wanted the archive. The mournful deflating honk of the bouncy castle, now lodged between two lampposts, reminded her of the commitment.

“No!” she croaked, raw. She looked at the disaster. Pride, reputation, the need for control. A thousand eyes. Talons dug into splintered stage wood, rough against the memory of smooth paper. A bead of sweat, sharp and metallic, trickled down her beak. Then she saw Bartholomew’s bewildered face, and a different heat — resolve — spread through her chest. A single trembling black feather detached and spiraled to the ground.

“Everyone,” she announced, voice surprisingly steady though her knees felt weak, “it seems my instructions were a little too specific.” Hush. Bartholomew looked confused. A small smile touched her beak. “But who needs perfectly placed balloons when you can have your own personalised confetti sky? And these jam tarts? They’re not a pyramid. They’re a delicious avalanche of fun!”

A nervous giggle, then another, growing bolder. Jonah the seal, who had been gamely attempting to redirect a stray bouncy castle with his nose, let out a happy rumbling bark.

Iris watched students chase falling confetti and scoop spilled tarts, turning disaster into an impromptu joyous food fight. Laughter grew, a warm infectious wave. Not the Fête she had planned. Undeniably fun.

Later, as the sun dipped, long shadows across slightly sticky jam-dotted grounds, Iris found herself laughing. A small echo of the confetti cannon popped in the distance. She did not flinch. She chuckled, light, carefree. Still the archivist. Also the raven who had named the avalanche. The rough stage under her talons felt less like a threat and more like a memory she might, one day, file under Founder’s Day, jam side up.
characters: Iris (raven school archivist), Bartholomew (badger assistant), Jonah (seal friend)
